This R markdown prepares data and figures contained within the Zion isotopes
analysis report aimed at understanding the age and travel paths of source water
to springs and seeps in the Main Canyon


### 1. Setup the workspace

```{r setup}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE,  message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval = TRUE)
source('setup.R')

mapviewOptions(fgb = FALSE,
               georaster = FALSE,
               basemaps = c("Esri.WorldTopoMap",
                            "Esri.WorldImagery"))

pal <- list(
  black = "black",
  gold = "#dca237",
  lightblue = "#6eb2e4",
  teal = "#459a74",
  yellow = "#eee461",
  darkblue = "#3070ad",
  orange = "#c66426",
  pink = "#c07da5",
  lightpink = "#ECD8E4"
)

nps_pal <- list(blue = "#85b6dc",
               red = "#c5312a",
               grey = "#a9a9a9",
               lightgrey = "#dcdcdc")


```

Define park using 4-digit NPS Unit Code. Codes for all parks can be found at:
<https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/foia/upload/NPS-Unit-List.xlsx>.

Download the park boundary from the NPS IRMA DataStore as an {sf} object.

```{r park_dat}
park <- "ZION"

# Get park geometry and metadata
park_boundary <- getParkBoundary(park = park)
state <- park_boundary$STATE
```

### 2. Identify the water supplies

##### ---- Water Supply Database

A water supply system database was created for this project using various NPS and public databases. The database contains a row for each water supply system and source of water (e.g., individual wells, diversions, and springs) associated with each supply.

```{r}

# Read in NPS Water Supply Geodatabase
source_table_locs <- get_wsd(fill_empty_coords = TRUE) %>%
  dplyr::filter(park_unit %in% c("ZION"))

```

### 3. Read in various datasets

Various park-specific datasets are available describing locations and other water system information for Zion.

##### ---- Site Locations

```{r site_data}

# Field samples collected/logged during the WFP 2025 Zion + CEBR + PIPE site
# visit (springs, wells, and streams together). This is the primary set of
# "our own" sample locations used throughout the rest of this document.
sample_locs <- read_csv("data/park/ZION/site_visit/2025_July_Zion_CEBR_PIPE_Sampling_Summary.csv") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), 
           crs = 4326, 
           remove = FALSE) %>%
  dplyr::filter(park == "ZION") %>%
  # Assign elevation to points using {elevatr} package
  get_elev_point(src = "aws", z = 14)

# Springs-only subset (drops wells and river/stream sites) -- used below to
# append spring locations onto the interpolated Navajo groundwater-level
# surface so springs and wells appear on the same elevation-contour map.
spring_locations <- sample_locs %>%
  dplyr::filter(!grepl("Well", location),
                !grepl("River", location))

# Statewide Utah springs inventory (SSI), spatially filtered to a 2 km buffer
# around the park boundary. This is an independent, third-party spring
# catalog used only as a QA/coverage check against our own site list (see
# map below and Figure 1 in Section 4) -- it is not otherwise joined into
# the analysis.
SSI_springs <- read_csv("data/park/ZION/SSI_SW_Utah.csv") %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude_dd","latitude_dd"), crs = 4269) %>%
  st_filter(park_boundary %>% st_buffer(2000)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(elevation_ft = elevation_m/0.348) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 4326)

mapview(SSI_springs) +
  mapview(sample_locs)

```


### 4. Geology and Aquifer Extent

With our water supplies identified, we can now delineate the source watershed and aquifer extent. We import the official NPS geology geodatabase directly (a coarser macrostrat-based lookup was tested during scoping and dropped in favor of this higher-resolution source).

```{r source_water}

# Import NPS GDB for zion
# https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/Reference/Profile/2305928
nps_gdb <- "data/park/ZION/geology/zion_geology_gdb_pro/zion_geology.gdb"
layers <- st_layers(nps_gdb)
nps_geo <- st_read(nps_gdb, layer = "zionglg")
nps_faults <- st_read(nps_gdb, layer = "zionflt")
nps_folds <- st_read(nps_gdb, layer = "zionfld")
nps_joints <- st_read(nps_gdb, layer = "zionjln")

# Quick QA preview of all mapped units
mapview(nps_geo, zcol = "SRC_SYM")

# Pull out select formations for plotting / recharge-area delineation.
# NOTE: `permian` and `volcanics` are defined but not currently added to the
# map below -- kept here for the recharge-area delineation work referenced
# in the section intro, not (yet) used for plotting.
navajo <- c("Jn", "Jnw", "Jnp", "Jnb", "Jnl")
kayenta <- c("Jk", "Jkt", "Jku", "Jks")
alluvium <- c("Qmt", "Qmts", "Qls", "Qmso", "Qath", "Qala")
temple_cap <- c("Jt", "Jtw", "Jts")
carmel <- c("Jc", "Jcw", "Jcp", "Jcx", "Jcc", "Jccu", "Jccl")
misc_alluv_colluv_eolian <- c("Qmsy", "Qre", "Qer", "Qcs", "Qces", "Qac")
permian <- c("Pkf","Pkh","Ptb","Ptw")
volcanics <- nps_geo %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("Qb", GLG_SYM)) %>% pull(GLG_SYM) %>% unique()

# Formation layers to draw on the site map, keyed by layer name so each
# formation's GLG_SYM codes, fill color, and transparency live in one place
# instead of one hand-written mapview() call per formation (previously ~50
# lines with only the filter/color/alpha differing). Add a new formation by
# adding one entry to each of the three lists below.
formation_groups <- list(
  "Alluvium"          = alluvium,
  "Carmel"            = carmel,
  "Temple Cap"        = temple_cap,
  "Navajo"            = navajo,
  "Kayenta"           = kayenta,
  "Alluv/Colluv/Eol"  = misc_alluv_colluv_eolian
)
formation_colors <- c(
  "Alluvium" = "yellow", "Carmel" = "darkblue", "Temple Cap" = "dodgerblue",
  "Navajo" = "hotpink", "Kayenta" = "darkred", "Alluv/Colluv/Eol" = "gold4"
)
formation_alpha <- c(
  "Alluvium" = 0.2, "Carmel" = 0.2, "Temple Cap" = 0.2,
  "Navajo" = 0.4, "Kayenta" = 0.4, "Alluv/Colluv/Eol" = 0.2
)

formation_maps <- purrr::imap(formation_groups, function(symbols, layer_name) {
  mapview(nps_geo %>% dplyr::filter(GLG_SYM %in% symbols),
          layer.name = layer_name,
          col.regions = formation_colors[[layer_name]],
          homebutton = FALSE,
          alpha.regions = formation_alpha[[layer_name]],
          lwd = 0)
}) %>%
  purrr::reduce(`+`)

# Site figure: water sources, park boundary, key formations, structure, and
# springs together in one map (used as the report's Figure 1 base layer)
a <-
  mapview(source_table_locs,
            col.regions = "red",
            alpha.regions = .4,
            cex = 5,
            layer.name = "Water Sources") +
    mapview(park_boundary,
            color = pal$teal,
            alpha.regions = 0,
            legend = FALSE,
            lwd = 4) +
  formation_maps +
  mapview(nps_faults,
          homebutton = FALSE,
          color = "black",
          layer.name = "Faults") +
  mapview(nps_joints,
          homebutton = FALSE,
          layer.name = "Joints",
          color = "gray40") +
  mapview(source_table_locs$watershed, alpha.regions = 0, layer.name = "Watersheds", lwd = 4, color = "dodgerblue") +
  mapview(SSI_springs, col.regions = "orange")

a

addStaticLabels(a,
                label = source_table_locs$source_name,
                noHide = TRUE,
                direction = 'right',
                textOnly = TRUE,
                textsize = "14px",
                style = list("color" = "black", "font-weight" = "bold"))

```

### 5. Surface Water and Groundwater Monitoring (NWIS)

The National Water Information System (NWIS) is a comprehensive database maintained by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) that provides access to water-related data for over 1.5 million sites across the United States and its territories. This data includes information on surface water, groundwater, springs, and atmospheric conditions.

Here, we download and read in various types of NWIS data in the vicinity of the park. For many parks, nearby NWIS sites are outside the park. We apply a buffer around the park boundary to capture as much data as possible.

Where possible, we prioritize stream gages deemed "reference" gages in the [GAGES-II database (Falcone, 2011)](https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70046617). We also prioritize gages that are closest to the park with the most complete period of record and delineate its associated watershed using the `get_nldi_basin()` function from the {nhdplusTools} package.

##### ---- NWIS Surface Water

For many parks, the nearest USGS stream gage is far away. Here we pull all
NWIS gages within 30 km of the park, then select only those classified as
"reference" gages in the
[GAGES-II database (Falcone, 2011)](https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70046617).
We delineate the watershed for each selected gage using `get_nldi_basin()` from
the {nhdplusTools} package.

```{r nwis, eval = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# --- 1. Site Selection ---
nwis <- listNWIS(aoi = park_boundary, dist = 30000)


# Filter for daily value (dv) data and the two target gages
nwis_select_stream_gage <- nwis %>%
  filter(
    data_type_cd == "dv",
    code         %in% c("00060", "00054"),
    site_no == "09405501"
  )

mapview(park_boundary, alpha.regions = 0) +
mapview(nwis_select_stream_gage) +
  mapview(source_table_locs, col.regions = "tomato")


# --- 2. Watershed Delineation and Area Calculation ---
nwis_select_watershed <- nwis_select_stream_gage$site_no %>%
  map_dfr(~ nldi_finder(site_no = .x)) %>%
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(nwis_select_stream_gage), by = "site_no") %>%
  mutate(
    drain_sqkm = geometry %>%
      st_area() %>%
      set_units("km^2") %>%
      as.numeric()
  )


# --- 4. Discharge Download and Depth-Normalized Conversion ---
# Convert from cfs to inches/day for area-normalized comparison
nwis_select_discharge <- readNWISdv(
    siteNumbers = nwis_select_stream_gage$site_no,
    parameterCd = "00060"
  ) %>%
  rename(discharge = X_00060_00003, date = Date) %>%
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(nwis_select_watershed), by = "site_no") %>%
  mutate(
    discharge_in_nwis = (86400 * 12 * discharge) / (drain_sqkm * 1.076e+7)
  )

# --- 5. Annual Summaries ---
nwis_select_discharge_an <- nwis_select_discharge %>%
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  group_by(year, site_no) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_q      = mean(discharge,         na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_q_unit = mean(discharge_in_nwis, na.rm = TRUE),
    peak_q      = max(discharge,          na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups     = "drop"
  )

ggarrange(
ggplot(nwis_select_discharge, aes(x = date, y = discharge)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Discharge (cfs)"),
ggplot(nwis_select_discharge_an,
       aes(x = year, y = 365.25*86400*mean_q*2.29569e-5)) +
    labs(x = "", y = "Annual Discharge (AF)") +
  geom_line())

```

##### ---- NWIS Groundwater

Groundwater monitoring wells near the park, filtered to the Navajo Sandstone
aquifer (`aqfr_cd == "220NVJO"` in the NWIS aquifer database) -- the same
formation the main-canyon springs discharge from.

```{r nwis_gw}
# --- 1. Filter for Groundwater Sites ---
# Start from the same `nwis` inventory pulled in the chunk above, keep only
# groundwater-level sites with at least one observation, attach aquifer
# metadata, then restrict to the Navajo Sandstone aquifer.
navajo_gw <- nwis %>%
  filter(data_type_cd == "gw", n_obs >= 1) %>%
  add_gw_meta() %>%
   dplyr::filter(aqfr_cd == "220NVJO") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(site_no = paste0("USGS-", site_no))

# --- 2. Retrieve and Process Water Level Records ---
# Depth-to-water (parameter 72019, ft below land surface) comes from two
# separate USGS endpoints that don't overlap in coverage: continuous daily
# values (read_waterdata_daily) and discrete field measurements
# (read_waterdata_field_measurements). Each site's mean depth is computed
# per source, then the two sources are stacked so every site contributes
# whichever record type it has.
navajo_gw_lev <-
  # First read daily data
  read_waterdata_daily(navajo_gw$site_no,
                       parameter_code = c(72019)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(site_no = monitoring_location_id) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(site_no, geometry) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(gw_depth_ft = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .groups = "keep") %>%
  bind_rows(
    # Now read field measurements
    read_waterdata_field_measurements(navajo_gw$site_no,
                                                parameter_code = c(72019)) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(site_no = monitoring_location_id) %>%
      dplyr::group_by(site_no, geometry) %>%
      dplyr::summarize(gw_depth_ft = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
                       .groups = "keep")
  ) 



navajo_sites <- navajo_gw_lev %>%
  group_by(site_no) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>%
  select(site_no, geometry) %>%
elevatr::get_elev_point(src = "aws", z = 14)

# Convert depth-to-water into a groundwater elevation (NAVD-style, ft) using
# each site's land-surface elevation, so wells and springs at different
# elevations become comparable/contourable.
navajo_gw_lev <- navajo_gw_lev %>%
  left_join(navajo_sites %>% st_drop_geometry(), by = "site_no") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(gw_elev_ft = (elevation/.3048) - gw_depth_ft)

# 
mapview(navajo_gw_lev,
        zcol = "gw_elev_ft")

navajo_gw_and_springs <- navajo_gw_lev %>%
  left_join(navajo_gw %>%
              st_drop_geometry(), by = "site_no") %>%
  bind_rows(spring_locations %>%
              dplyr::mutate(gw_elev_ft = (elevation/.3048),
                            site_no = location) %>%
              select(site_no, gw_elev_ft))

mapview(navajo_gw_and_springs,
        zcol = "gw_elev_ft")



# --- Helper: interpolate point groundwater levels to a raster surface via
# inverse-distance weighting (IDW) and return elevation contours as sf.
# Written as a reusable function (point set + contour interval as arguments)
# rather than inline code, so any future second surface (e.g. a local
# well-network contour) can reuse it without duplicating this ~30-line block.
interpolate_gw_contours <- function(points_sf, value_col, proj_crs = 26913,
                                     cell_res = 100, contour_interval = 50) {

  points_proj <- st_transform(points_sf, crs = proj_crs)

  grid <- raster::raster(
    ext = raster::extent(points_proj),
    resolution = cell_res,
    crs = st_crs(points_proj)$wkt
  )
  grid_spdf <- as(grid, "SpatialPixelsDataFrame")

  idw_surface <- gstat::idw(
    formula = stats::as.formula(paste(value_col, "~ 1")),
    locations = as(points_proj, "Spatial"),
    newdata = grid_spdf,
    idp = 2
  )

  idw_raster <- raster::raster(idw_surface)

  contour_levels <- seq(
    floor(min(raster::values(idw_raster), na.rm = TRUE) / contour_interval) * contour_interval,
    ceiling(max(raster::values(idw_raster), na.rm = TRUE) / contour_interval) * contour_interval,
    by = contour_interval
  )

  raster::rasterToContour(idw_raster, levels = contour_levels) %>%
    st_as_sf() %>%
    st_transform(crs = 4326)
}

navajo_contours <- interpolate_gw_contours(navajo_gw_and_springs, "gw_elev_ft", contour_interval = 500)

mapview(navajo_gw_and_springs, zcol = "gw_elev_ft") +
  mapview(navajo_contours, zcol = "level") +
  mapview(park_boundary, alpha.regions = 0, color = "black", lwd = 3) +
  mapview(nps_joints, color = "gray30") +
  mapview(nps_faults, color = "black")

```

### 6. Groundwater Age and Recharge Source

This is the central technical question for the Zion main canyon assessment:
are the Navajo Formation springs sourced primarily from recent (decadal)
meteoric water, as at Blowhard Spring in the CEBR assessment, or from an
older, larger, more slowly-circulating reservoir that would be substantially
buffered against short-term climate variability? We use tritium, carbon-14,
and stable water isotopes together to address this, followed by a
travel-time cross-check based on the regional hydraulic gradient.

##### ---- Tritium

Tritium (³H), a radioactive isotope of hydrogen, is a valuable tool for dating 
groundwater, specifically for determining the age of water that has infiltrated 
the ground within the last 70 years or so. By measuring tritium levels in spring
water that was recently discharged from groundwater, we can estimate the time 
since the water was recharged from the surface.

Download precipitation tritium data from nearest Global Network of Isotopes in 
Precipitation (GNIP) station. This data is free but requires users to create an
account: <https://nucleus.iaea.org/wiser> The nearest stations are Salt Lake 
City, Albuquerque, Santa Maria, and Phoenix.

Lindsey et al., 2019: Tritium as an Indicator of Modern, Mixed, and Premodern 
Groundwater Age <https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2019/5090/sir20195090.pdf> This paper
describes steps for calculating thresholds for groundwater age ranges.

```{r tritium}

# Define constants and functions

# Tritium half life (years)
h3_half <- 12.32

# Function to model radioactive decay
decay <- function(init_conc, elapsed_time, half_life) {
  init_conc * 0.5^(elapsed_time / half_life)
}


# Import NPS spring tritium + carbon-14 samples (Kimball & Christensen
# historical samples plus 2025 resampling). Tritium and carbon-14-corrected
# age live in the SAME source file, one row per field sample/analysis, so
# read it once here into `zion_samples` and derive both the tritium working
# table (this chunk) and the carbon-14 working table (`c14_nps`, further
# below) from it -- avoids reading/parsing the same CSV twice.
zion_samples <- read_csv("data/park/ZION/Tritium/Park_Samples/Zion_Tritium.csv") %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(date = mdy(date),
                tritium = as.numeric(tritium),
                c14_corr_age = as.numeric(c14_corr_age))

tritium_nps <- zion_samples %>%
  drop_na(tritium) %>%
  select(location, date, tritium, cond)

# Import and clean tritium precipitation data from nearby GNIP stations
tritium_gnip <- list.files(path = "data/park/ZION/Tritium/GNIP WISER/",
                           full.names = TRUE) %>%
  map_dfr(., read_xlsx) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  dplyr::filter(measurand_symbol == "H3") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(sample_date = as.Date(sample_date)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(biannual_date = floor_date(sample_date, "6 months")) %>%
  group_by(sample_site_name, biannual_date) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(measurand_amount = mean(measurand_amount, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .groups = "keep") %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() 


# ---- Nearby USGS discrete water-quality (tritium) samples -----------------
# Migrated off dataRetrieval::readWQPqw() and the old listNWIS()-based "qw"
# site discovery, both retired along with the legacy NWIS web services.
# Discrete/water-quality samples now live entirely outside the time-series
# API listNWIS() uses -- they're in USGS's separate Samples system, queried
# here with read_waterdata_samples() directly (not via `nwis`/listNWIS() at
# all; see listNWIS.R's migration notes for why "qw" rows no longer appear
# there).
#
# Step 1: find nearby sites (same park-boundary buffer distance used for
# `nwis` above) that have reported a tritium measurement. `characteristic =
# "Tritium"` and `siteTypeName` are both controlled-vocabulary values --
# confirm these are still the exact registered strings with
# `dataRetrieval::check_waterdata_sample_params("characteristics")` and
# `check_waterdata_sample_params("sitetype")$typeLongName` if this comes back
# empty.
park_bbox_4326 <- park_boundary %>%
  sf::st_buffer(30000) %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
  sf::st_bbox() %>%
  as.numeric()

tritium_wqp_sites <- dataRetrieval::read_waterdata_samples(
    boundingBox = park_bbox_4326,
    siteTypeName = c("Stream", "Well", "Spring"),
    characteristic = "Tritium",
    dataType = "locations",
    dataProfile = "site"
  ) %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

# Step 2: pull the actual tritium results for those sites. "narrow" is the
# slimmed-down results profile (the default "fullphyschem" profile returns
# ~190 columns per result).
tritium_wqp_raw <- dataRetrieval::read_waterdata_samples(
    monitoringLocationIdentifier = tritium_wqp_sites$location_identifier,
    characteristic = "Tritium",
    dataType = "results",
    dataProfile = "narrow"
  ) %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

# TODO: confirm column names before trusting the conversion below --
# `read_waterdata_samples(dataProfile = "narrow")`'s exact column names for
# the measured value/unit were not independently verifiable while writing
# this (no live R session in this pass). Expected, based on USGS's own
# examples: result_measure (numeric value), result_measure_unit (unit
# string), activity_start_date_time. Run
# `dplyr::glimpse(tritium_wqp_raw)` first and adjust the names below (and
# the T.U./pCi/L strings, which may also differ) if they don't match.
tritium_wqp <- tritium_wqp_raw %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    tritium_tu = dplyr::case_when(
      result_measure_unit == "T.U."   ~ result_measure,
      result_measure_unit == "pCi/L"  ~ result_measure / 3.22,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    activity_start_date = as.Date(activity_start_date_time)
  )


# ---- Moving modern & premodern thresholds ---------------------------------
# USGS Step 1/2 define both thresholds relative to "the date of the
# groundwater 3H sample." Our NPS samples span 1988-89 AND 2025, so a single
# threshold pinned to one reference date badly misrepresents whichever end of
# that range it wasn't computed for. Instead we define both thresholds as
# FUNCTIONS of a target date, then evaluate them either at each sample's own
# date (for classification) or across a continuous date grid (to draw them
# as curves that shift/decay through time on the plot).

# Identify each GNIP station's bomb-peak date so the modern threshold only
# uses POST-peak precipitation values, per USGS Step 1 ("minimum post-peak
# concentration"). NOTE: for a station whose record only starts after the
# real ~1963-64 bomb peak (the code comment says Albuquerque has no data
# before ~2000), its "peak" here is just the max of its own truncated
# record, not the true atmospheric peak -- worth a visual sanity check
# against the individual station curves.
gnip_peaks <- tritium_gnip %>%
  group_by(sample_site_name) %>%
  dplyr::slice_max(measurand_amount, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  dplyr::transmute(sample_site_name, peak_date = biannual_date,
                    peak_value = measurand_amount) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()

tritium_gnip <- tritium_gnip %>%
  dplyr::left_join(gnip_peaks, by = "sample_site_name") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(post_peak = biannual_date > peak_date)


# ---- Per-station thresholds -> station-to-station RANGE -------------------
# The pooled modern_threshold_fun()/premodern_threshold_fun() above answer
# "what's the most conservative threshold across all 4 GNIP stations
# combined." Computing the same thing PER STATION and taking the min/max
# across stations at each date instead gives an honest visual range for how
# much the threshold depends on which station's precipitation record you're
# trusting, rather than hiding that choice inside a single line.

safe_min <- function(x) if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
safe_max <- function(x) if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
safe_mean <- function(x) if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)


# Pooled thresholds for classifying individual samples at their EXACT date
# (not just the 3-month grid used for the ribbon). Defined as "whichever
# station gives the most conservative (lowest) value at this date" -- same
# min-across-everything philosophy as before, and guarantees these match
# threshold_curve's central line exactly rather than duplicating the logic.
modern_threshold_fun <- function(target_date) {
  safe_mean(purrr::map_dbl(stations, 
                           ~ modern_threshold_station_fun(target_date, .x)))
}
premodern_threshold_fun <- function(target_date) {
  safe_min(purrr::map_dbl(stations, 
                          ~ premodern_threshold_station_fun(target_date, .x)))
}

modern_threshold_station_fun <- function(target_date, station) {
  tritium_gnip %>%
    dplyr::filter(sample_site_name == station, post_peak,
                  biannual_date <= target_date) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(decayed = decay(measurand_amount,
                                   as.numeric(target_date - biannual_date) / 365.25,
                                   h3_half)) %>%
    dplyr::pull(decayed) %>%
    safe_min()
}

# ---- Upper-bound alternative for the modern endmember ----------------------
# modern_threshold_station_fun() above answers "what's the LOWEST plausible
# concentration for water recharged since the bomb peak" (the minimum
# post-peak precipitation value, decayed forward) -- deliberately
# conservative, and used as-is for MODERN/MIXED/PREMODERN classification and
# as the primary mixing-model endmember below. But it understates how high a
# "modern" (post-1953) sample COULD plausibly read if it happened to
# recharge near the actual 1963-64 bomb-pulse peak rather than at some later,
# already-decayed point in the record. Decaying each station's own peak
# concentration forward to the target date gives that upper bound instead.
# Because the peak was roughly 2-3 orders of magnitude higher than any
# post-peak precipitation value, this upper-bound endmember comes out
# roughly 60x higher than modern_threshold_station_fun() at any given target
# date -- so it is used only to widen the mixing model's estimated
# young-fraction range downward (see tritium_mixing_model chunk), not to
# replace the primary threshold used for classification or the primary
# (upper-bound-endmember) young-fraction point estimate.
modern_threshold_peak_station_fun <- function(target_date, station) {
  peak_row <- gnip_peaks %>% dplyr::filter(sample_site_name == station)
  if (nrow(peak_row) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  decay(peak_row$peak_value,
        as.numeric(target_date - peak_row$peak_date) / 365.25,
        h3_half)
}
modern_threshold_peak_fun <- function(target_date) {
  safe_mean(purrr::map_dbl(stations,
                            ~ modern_threshold_peak_station_fun(target_date, .x)))
}

# NA for any station with no data in the 2004-2012 reference window --
# currently that's every station except Albuquerque, so this ribbon may be
# degenerate (near-zero width) unless other data is added.
mean_2008_2012_by_station <- tritium_gnip %>%
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::between(year(biannual_date), 2004, 2012)) %>%
  group_by(sample_site_name) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(mean_conc = mean(measurand_amount, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .groups = "drop") %>%
  tibble::deframe()

premodern_threshold_station_fun <- function(target_date, station,
                                            premodern_ref_date = as.Date("1953-01-01")) {
  base_conc <- purrr::pluck(mean_2008_2012_by_station, station, .default = NA_real_)
  if (is.na(base_conc)) return(NA_real_)
  decay(base_conc, as.numeric(target_date - premodern_ref_date) / 365.25, h3_half)
}

stations <- unique(tritium_gnip$sample_site_name)

threshold_curve_by_station <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  date = seq(as.Date("1965-01-01"),
             max(tritium_nps$date, tritium_wqp$activity_start_date, na.rm = TRUE),
             by = "3 months"),
  station = stations
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    modern_threshold    = purrr::map2_dbl(date, station, 
                                          modern_threshold_station_fun),
    premodern_threshold = purrr::map2_dbl(date, station, 
                                          premodern_threshold_station_fun)
  )

# Collapse across stations to (a) the min/max range for the ribbon, and
# (b) the same pooled/conservative summary line you already had (kept under
# the original names so the annotate() lookups below still work unchanged).
threshold_curve <- threshold_curve_by_station %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(
    modern_threshold_min    = safe_min(modern_threshold),
    modern_threshold_max    = safe_max(modern_threshold),
    modern_threshold        = safe_mean(modern_threshold),   
    premodern_threshold_min = safe_min(premodern_threshold),
    premodern_threshold_max = safe_max(premodern_threshold),
    premodern_threshold     = safe_mean(premodern_threshold), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Evaluate both thresholds at EACH NPS sample's own date -- this is what
# makes classification correct for both the 1988-89 batch and the 2025
# batch instead of forcing everything through one 1989 threshold.
tritium_nps <- tritium_nps %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    modern_threshold   = purrr::map_dbl(date, modern_threshold_fun),
    premodern_threshold = purrr::map_dbl(date, premodern_threshold_fun),
    classification = dplyr::case_when(
      tritium >= modern_threshold    ~ "Modern",
      tritium <= premodern_threshold ~ "Premodern",
      TRUE                            ~ "Mixed"
    )
  )

# Same thresholds evaluated at each WQP sample's own date, if you want to
# classify those too (not just eyeball them against a curve).
tritium_wqp <- tritium_wqp %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    modern_threshold    = purrr::map_dbl(activity_start_date, modern_threshold_fun),
    premodern_threshold = purrr::map_dbl(activity_start_date, premodern_threshold_fun),
    classification = dplyr::case_when(
      tritium_tu >= modern_threshold    ~ "Modern",
      tritium_tu <= premodern_threshold ~ "Premodern",
      TRUE                                ~ "Mixed"
    )
  )

tritium_plot <- ggplot(tritium_gnip) +
  geom_line(
    aes(x = biannual_date, y = measurand_amount, color = sample_site_name),
```

Key pattern: the 2025 samples (East Entrance Well, Birch sediment trap, Lower
Grotto sand trap) are all at or near the analytical detection floor
(0.001-0.2 TU) and below the threshold for pre-modern waters. This is consistent
with water that predates atmospheric nuclear testing (pre-1950s recharge). The 
1988-89 samples at The Grotto, Weeping Rock, and Refrigerator Spring 
(4.5-9.3 TU) sit at or below the modern threshold for that period, suggesting a 
mix of old water with at most a modest young-water fraction. Echo Canyon Spring 
is the exception (33-46 TU), indicating a distinctly younger, faster-responding
system -- plausibly a different, shallower flow path than the main canyon Navajo springs.

```{r seasonal_variation_of_tritium}
# ---- Seasonal variation at repeat-sampled locations ------------------------
# Do we need to decay-correct first? Yes -- raw values conflate any true
# seasonal signal with ordinary radioactive decay between sample dates. The
# choice of reference date doesn't change the SHAPE of the seasonal pattern
# (decay-correcting to any single common date preserves each location's
# relative differences), it only sets a common absolute scale -- we use the
# most recent sample date in the dataset so this column is also usable
# elsewhere (e.g., alongside the modern/premodern classification above).

seasonal_ref_date <- max(tritium_nps$date, na.rm = TRUE)

tritium_nps_seasonal <- tritium_nps %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    decayed_to_ref = decay(tritium,
                            as.numeric(seasonal_ref_date - date) / 365.25,
                            h3_half),
    sample_month = lubridate::month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
    season = dplyr::case_when(
      lubridate::month(date) %in% c(12, 1, 2)  ~ "Winter",
      lubridate::month(date) %in% c(3, 4, 5)   ~ "Spring",
      lubridate::month(date) %in% c(6, 7, 8)   ~ "Summer",
      lubridate::month(date) %in% c(9, 10, 11) ~ "Fall"
    )
  )

# Only locations with samples from more than one DISTINCT date carry any
# seasonal information -- same-day replicate/split samples don't.
locations_multi <- tritium_nps_seasonal %>%
  group_by(location) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(
    n_samples = dplyr::n(),
    n_dates   = dplyr::n_distinct(date),
    months_sampled = paste(unique(as.character(sample_month)), collapse = ", "),
    date_range_days = as.numeric(diff(range(date))),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::filter(n_dates > 1)

locations_multi

tritium_nps_seasonal_multi <- tritium_nps_seasonal %>%
  dplyr::filter(location %in% locations_multi$location)

# One panel per location, decay-corrected tritium by sample month. Free
# y-scales since absolute tritium levels differ a lot spring to spring --
# the question is the SHAPE across months at a given spring, not comparing
# magnitudes across springs.
tritium_seasonal_plot <- ggplot(tritium_nps_seasonal_multi, aes(x = sample_month, y = decayed_to_ref)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = "-", size = 10, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ location, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Tritium (TU), decay-corrected",
       title = "Seasonal variation in tritium at repeat-sampled springs",
       subtitle = paste0("Decay-corrected to ", format(seasonal_ref_date, "%Y-%m-%d"))) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

    .groups = "drop"
```

```{r tritium_mixing_model}

# ---- Two-component mixing model: estimated young (modern) fraction --------
# Uses the per-sample, date-matched modern_threshold/premodern_threshold
# already computed for classification -- no additional decay correction
# needed since those are already valid AS OF each sample's own date.
# Standard conservative-tracer linear mixing: 0 = pure premodern endmember,
# 1 = pure modern endmember. NOTE: because modern_threshold is deliberately
# the MINIMUM (most conservative) post-peak value, this tends to overstate
# the young fraction -- treat as an upper-bound estimate, not a point
# estimate. Values outside [0,1] are kept (not clipped) since they're
# informative: they mean a sample is more extreme than either endmember.
tritium_nps <- tritium_nps %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    young_fraction = (tritium - premodern_threshold) / (modern_threshold - premodern_threshold),
    young_fraction_capped = pmin(1, pmax(0, young_fraction)),
    fraction_flag = dplyr::case_when(
      young_fraction > 1 ~ "Exceeds MT",
      young_fraction < 0 ~ "Below PMT",
      TRUE               ~ "Within mixing range"
    )
  )

# ---- Widened lower bound: modern endmember decayed from the bomb PEAK ------
# young_fraction/young_fraction_capped above already use the most
# conservative (lowest-plausible) modern endmember, which is treated as the
# PRIMARY estimate. This block adds a second, much higher modern endmember --
# each station's own peak concentration decayed forward to the sample date --
# to see how low the young fraction COULD plausibly go if a sample happened
# to contain water recharged right at 1963-64 bomb-peak concentrations
# instead. Because the peak is roughly 2 orders of magnitude higher than the
# minimum post-peak value, this pushes young_fraction_lo_capped down close to
# 0 for nearly every sample -- it is used only as an extended LOWER bound on
# the mixing-model uncertainty range (tritium_young_frac_by_location's
# young_frac_min, below), not as an alternative point estimate. The primary
# point estimate stays anchored to young_fraction_capped: the strong,
# repeated seasonal swings documented in Section 3.4/3.5 (e.g., Weeping
# Rock's young fraction moving from 60% to 94% between sampling rounds within
# a single year) are much easier to reconcile with a modern component that is
# genuinely close to today's background atmospheric concentration than with
# a static, decades-old bomb-peak-derived admixture, which would not be
# expected to produce that kind of short-term variability.
tritium_nps <- tritium_nps %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    modern_threshold_peak = purrr::map_dbl(date, modern_threshold_peak_fun),
    young_fraction_lo = (tritium - premodern_threshold) / (modern_threshold_peak - premodern_threshold),
    young_fraction_lo_capped = pmin(1, pmax(0, young_fraction_lo))
  )

# Location-level tritium summary (one row per location): young-fraction
# mean/min/max plus the set of classification labels seen across repeat
# dates. Computed here (immediately after young_fraction_capped exists)
# rather than down in the carbon-14 chunks, since both the carbon-14 error
# bars and the multi-evidence summary table need it and it belongs
# logically with the rest of the tritium mixing-model output, not
# duplicated per consumer. young_frac_mean and young_frac_max are unchanged
# (primary, upper-bound-endmember estimate); young_frac_min is widened to
# the peak-endmember lower bound above, so the reported range reflects both
# sample-to-sample variability AND modern-endmember uncertainty.
tritium_young_frac_by_location <- tritium_nps %>%
  drop_na(young_fraction_capped) %>%
  group_by(location) %>%
  summarize(
    young_frac_mean = mean(young_fraction_capped, na.rm = TRUE),
    young_frac_min  = min(young_fraction_lo_capped, na.rm = TRUE),
    young_frac_max  = max(young_fraction_capped, na.rm = TRUE),
    young_frac_min_primary = min(young_fraction_capped, na.rm = TRUE),
    tritium_category = paste(sort(unique(classification)), collapse = ", "),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

tritium_nps_seasonal <- tritium_nps_seasonal %>%
  dplyr::left_join(
    tritium_nps %>% dplyr::select(location, date, young_fraction),
    by = c("location", "date")
  )

# Plot estimated young fraction by month, one panel per repeat-sampled
# location -- same seasonal question as before, but expressed as "fraction
# of recently-recharged water" rather than raw/decay-corrected TU.
young_frac_plot <- ggplot(tritium_nps_seasonal_multi %>%
         dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(tritium_nps, location, date, young_fraction_capped),
                           by = c("location", "date")),
       aes(x = sample_month, y = young_fraction_capped)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = 3, color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = "-", size = 10, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ location) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimated young (modern) fraction",
       title = "Seasonal variation in estimated young-water fraction") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

young_frac_plot

ggsave(plot = young_frac_plot,
       filename = "data/park/ZION/Tritium/tritium_young_seasonal.tif", dpi = 600, width = 7, height = 4)
```
